At that time, the World-Honored One was on the summit of Vulture Peak at the great place for walking meditation, together with his attendant Ānanda;
from afar, he praised Mañjuśrī, saying:
“Excellent, excellent, Mañjuśrī!
You have well expounded this dharma-gate of the most supreme skillful means of diligence for bodhisattvas, just as you have described it.”
When these words were praised, their sound pervaded the trichiliocosm, and the entire earth shook in six ways.

At that time, immeasurable devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans—including Śakra Devendra, Mahābrahmā, and the Four Great Kings—all followed the sound and together went to the place where the Buddha was. They paid respectful homage at his feet and withdrew to stand to one side, where they all addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!...”
"Just now we heard the Tathāgata’s voice of praise, 'Excellent! resound throughout the great trichiliocosm, causing the earth to tremble everywhere. We do not yet know whom the Tathāgata has praised.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the great assembly:
"I have just now praised Mañjuśrī."
At that time, the great assembly again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One! Where is Mañjuśrī now?"
The Buddha said:
"He is on the road by the eastern gate of Rājagṛha, expounding the sublime Dharma for the great assembly together with the girl Suvarṇavarṇā.
If you wish to hear the Dharma, you should go there."

At that time, all the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans—including Śakra Devendra, Mahābrahmā, and the Four Great Kings—having heard the Buddha’s teaching, went together to the place where Mañjuśrī was. Each manifested their own extraordinary radiance and rained down exquisite celestial flowers over Rājagṛha and the entire great assembly.
At that time, the entire assembly of humans and devas were all able to see one another without any obstruction.
All the people of Rājagṛha, seeing the hosts of devas and the wondrous flowers, followed one another to the place where Mañjuśrī was.
At that time, King Ajātaśatru, adorned with great majesty and power, set out for the place where Mañjuśrī was, accompanied by his fourfold army and the ladies of the harem.

At that time, all the princes, ministers, elders, and sons of householders within the city, seeing that the daughter Suvarṇavarṇā’s mind abided in tranquil extinction, all abandoned their defiled minds; their five faculties became pure, they were endowed with shame and remorse, and were no longer subject to afflictions.
At that time, Mañjuśrī, seeing that this great assembly had no defiled thoughts toward the girl Suvarṇavarṇā, asked her:
"Where have you placed your afflictions now, such that these princes and even the sons of householders do not give rise to defiled thoughts?"
The Golden-Hued Woman said:
"All afflictions and the afflictions of sentient beings abide on the shore of wisdom and liberation, within the equality of the suchness of the Dharma-realm."
Those afflictions neither arise nor cease, nor are they established; I know the essential nature of the afflictions thus, and I see them with correct vision in this way.
Mañjuśrī said to the girl Suvarṇavarṇā,
“What is the essential nature of afflictions?
The girl Suvarṇavarṇā replied:

"All evil discursive thoughts are the very nature of afflictions; because they take impurity as their object, afflictions arise. Because of pure discursive thoughts, afflictions are merely adventitious. Therefore, afflictions do not combine with the wisdom of emptiness, nor do they combine with signlessness or wishlessness."

Just as when a great venomous snake fixes its gaze upon a person, that person is instantly destroyed; yet if a wise person takes agada medicine and goes to where that snake is, the snake loses its venom upon smelling the scent of the medicine, such that even if a child were to provoke it in various ways, it could not cause harm.

Mañjuśrī! In the past, because of my evil discursive thoughts, a perverted mind arose and I was consumed by the fire of afflictions. I was attached to this body, not realizing that it is like foam, like a flame, like an illusion, like a transformation, or like a dream. To experience the pleasures of the five desires is like licking a knife coated with honey; the fool craves the flavor without perceiving that his tongue will be wounded.

Furthermore, it is like dew on the grass that vanishes upon seeing the sun; [beings] do not know that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent and swift, they do not know that the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) are invariably suffering, they do not know that the nature of their own bodies is impure, they do not know that all phenomena (*dharma*) are devoid of the various distinctions of "self" and "what belongs to self," they do not know that while they themselves see nothing, they cause others to be shrouded in darkness, and they do not know that while they are bound themselves, they further bind others.

"Before I heard the Dharma, I did not attain liberation from these phenomena; now that I have heard the Dharma and attained wisdom, I have attained liberation from all afflictions. Therefore, no sentient beings give rise to thoughts of lust toward my body."
“Mañjuśrī! Just as light does not coexist with darkness, so too afflictions do not abide in one whose mind is free from desire.
When the Golden Girl had finished speaking these teachings to Mañjuśrī, she addressed him, saying:

“A great assembly of devas and humans has gathered; we pray that you, out of compassion and endowed with the power of Dharma, will reveal and instruct these devas and humans so that they may know the essential nature of all afflictions. Having known this essential nature, may you give rise to a heart of pity for all sentient beings, and for the sake of their attaining peace and security, resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.”
Then Mañjuśrī spoke again: "The essential nature of these afflictions is difficult to believe and difficult to understand. Why is this?"
Because this nature of affliction is itself bodhi.
For example, as long as fire has not emerged, it cannot burn wood; likewise, one who does not give rise to afflictions does not undergo birth and death within saṃsāra.
Just as once fire has emerged it can burn wood, so too when evil thoughts arise, one wanders through birth and death.

Just as a fire burning a great heap of grass and wood is difficult to extinguish because of its intensity, so too the poisonous mind of wrong views, conjoined with the afflictions, blazes fiercely within the three realms, constantly burning without respite.
Just as fire cannot burn without fuel, so too, when one is free from evil views, the afflictions do not arise within the three realms.

Just as fire, even if it burns for hundreds or thousands of years, provides no benefit and does not increase, so too is the blazing fire of the afflictions; even after hundreds or thousands of years, it provides no benefit and does not increase.
Just as when a fire is extinguished it does not go to any particular location, so too when wisdom extinguishes all afflictions, it likewise does not go to any particular location.
Just as no one is able to enter a fierce fire, so too this naturally pure nature cannot be defiled by the arising of adventitious afflictions.
At that time, Mañjuśrī asked the girl Suvarṇavarṇā,
"How do you perceive the body?
The girl Suvarṇavarṇā replied:
"It is like seeing the moon in water.
He asked again,
"How does one see the five aggregates?"
The woman said,
"It is like seeing a person created by the Buddha’s transformation.
He asked again:
“How does one perceive the eighteen realms?
The woman replied,
“It is like perceiving the kalpa-fire burning all the worlds.”
He asked again:
"How does one perceive the twelve bases?
The woman replied:
“It is like performing no karmic action.
He asked again:
“How does one view the fourfold assembly?”
The woman replied,
“It is like seeing the space above.
He asked again:
“How does one contemplate one’s own body?
The Golden-Hued Woman replied,
“One knows that it is born from the union of father and mother.”
He asked again: "How do you see my body?
The woman replied:
"It is like a blind person seeing forms.
He asked again,
"Do you now listen to this Dharma?"
The Golden-Colored Woman replied,
“It is like a phantom person listening to the Dharma.
He asked again:
“Have you resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
The girl Suvarṇavarṇā replied, “I have already resolved; I do not resolve it again.”
He asked again:
"Do you practice the perfection of giving?
The woman replied:
"Neither practice nor abandon within the afflictions.
He asked again:
"Have you fulfilled the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā)?"
The woman said:
"Fullness is like the fullness of space.
He asked again:
“Do you cultivate the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā)?
The woman replied,
“I have already cultivated it, just as all sentient beings are neither born nor produced.”
He asked again,
"Have you resolved upon the *vīryapāramitā*?
The woman replied:
“Having already set out, it is as all dharmas are unattainable.
He asked again:
“Do you abide in the dhyāna-pāramitā?”
The woman said:
"I abide; I abide as one abides within the dharma-realm.
He asked again:
“Have you fulfilled the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā)?
The woman replied,
“I have fulfilled it.”
"What is meant by 'fulfillment'?
It is because of the wisdom of skillful means that neither increases nor decreases.
He asked again:
“Do you cultivate loving-kindness?
The woman replied,
“I have already cultivated it, just as all sentient beings do not arise.”
He asked again:
"Where should one seek the great compassion of a bodhisattva?
The woman replied:
"Seek it within the afflictions of all sentient beings.
Why is this? If sentient beings were without afflictions, bodhisattvas would not resolve to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
Mañjuśrī asked, "Where should one seek the mind of joy?
The woman replied:
"Seek it within a mind of supreme faith, purity, and joy in bodhi.
Mañjuśrī asked: "How does a bodhisattva fulfill the mind of equanimity?"
The woman said:
"To abandon all strife and contention among sentient beings is called 'fulfillment'; to remain far removed from all disputes and arguments regarding phenomena is therefore called 'fulfillment'."
Mañjuśrī asked, “What is meant by ‘contentious debate’?
The girl replied:
"If a bodhisattva says of himself:
'I shall abandon all afflictions and deliver all sentient beings,' this is called contentious debate."
Mañjuśrī spoke again: "With whom are you debating?
The woman replied:
"All non-Buddhists. He asked again:
"Who are the non-Buddhists?"
The woman said:
"To comply with and tolerate the false teachings of others is called being an outsider (tīrthika).
Furthermore, from what does the bodhisattva’s mind of patience arise?"
The woman said:
"It arises from the affliction and disturbance caused by all sentient beings. Why is this?"
If one does not cause disturbance, it is because the mind of resentment does not arise.

If a bodhisattva undergoes the abuse, scolding, beating, and humiliation of sentient beings, yet their mind remains like the earth, giving rise to no malice or resentment, this is called patience (*kṣānti*).
Mañjuśrī asked, "What is malice? The woman replied:
"One who harbors hatred can destroy the wholesome karma created over a hundred kalpas;
this is called 'hatred. He asked again: 'What is non-hatred?'"
The woman said:
"If one encounters all objects of affliction without any obstruction, this is called being free from ill will. Mañjuśrī said:
“How does a bodhisattva achieve victory in debate?
The woman replied, “A bodhisattva achieves victory by being without conceptual discrimination and without apprehension regarding all phenomena; this is what is called victory.”
Mañjuśrī spoke again:
"How does a bodhisattva remain far removed from the enmity of Māra?
The woman replied:
"Although a bodhisattva manifests the activities of Māra, they remain unstained by them; this is what is called 'being far removed from the enemy Māra.

Why is this? Although a bodhisattva manifests the afflictions of the five aggregates (pañca-skandha), they do not enter into union with those five aggregates and afflictions, because their essential nature is unstained."

Although a bodhisattva manifests birth and death to teach and transform sentient beings, they know that all phenomena have no coming or going; thus, although they speak of the path of the celestial Māras for the sake of sentient beings, within their own omniscience they have personally distanced themselves from "I" and "mine."
Mañjuśrī asked, “How does a bodhisattva transform sentient beings?
The woman replied:
"One should cultivate the Prajñāpāramitā of skillful means, for it is capable of transforming and teaching others.
Mañjuśrī spoke again:
"How does a bodhisattva dwell securely among all sentient beings?"
The woman said,
"Just as the Bodhisattva abides within wisdom, so too do all sentient beings abide. Mañjuśrī said:
“Daughter! When the entire assembly heard you preach the Dharma, their hearts were filled with love and joy, and they came to revere you.
The girl said:
“Mañjuśrī! One should not pay respect and make offerings in such a manner; those who offer in this way do not truly perform an offering. Why is this?
If one perceives one's own body, another's body, or any phenomenon that can be described, it is not called making an offering;
if one does not perceive one's own body, another's body, or any phenomenon, this is called making an offering.
"Thus, to be without hearing and without attachment is called listening to the Dharma,
and it is also called making offerings. Mañjuśrī asked, "What is the offering of the Dharma?"
The woman said:

"If one contemplates the body as a dream, the speaker as an illusion, and the Dharma heard as an echo, and having thus gained faith, does not form dualistic notions regarding liberation—this is called the offering of Dharma."
Mañjuśrī asked, "How does one listen to the Dharma?
The woman replied:
"To practice according to what has been taught is called 'listening to the Dharma.

By the supernatural power of the youth Mañjuśrī and by the power of her own past roots of goodness and wisdom, the girl Suvarṇavarṇā preached the Dharma in accordance with the truth within that assembly.
At that time, while the girl Suvarṇavarṇā was preaching this Dharma, there were among the assembly one billion people who resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Furthermore, there were five hundred gods and humans from the past who had deeply planted roots of goodness, who attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Thirty-three thousand devas and humans were distanced from dust and freed from defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye.

The girl Suvarṇavarṇā, with a purified mind and great joy, attained the patience that accords with the Dharma (*anulomikī kṣānti*). Having attained this patient acceptance, she prostrated at the feet of Mañjuśrī and, feeling deep shame and remorse for herself, spoke these words:
"Regarding the True Dharma, I am like one who is already dead; I only pray that you will compassionately grant me permission to leave the household life."
Mañjuśrī said: "For a bodhisattva who has left the household life, it is not by shaving one's own head that one is called 'one who has gone forth. Why is this?"
If one can generate great diligence in order to eliminate the afflictions of all sentient beings, this is called the renunciation of a bodhisattva.

It is not by merely donning dyed robes upon one's own body that one is called "renounced"; rather, diligently severing the defiled minds of the three poisons within sentient beings is what is called renunciation.

It is not merely maintaining one's own observance of the precepts that is called "leaving home"; rather, it is the ability to cause those who have violated the prohibitions to dwell securely in pure precepts that is called "leaving home.

It is not merely sitting alone in contemplation in an araṇya hermitage that is called "leaving home"; rather, it is the ability to use wisdom and skillful means to transform women—who are caught in the flow and turning of birth and death—so that they attain liberation, that is called "leaving home."

It is not by guarding the precepts for one's own sake that one is called a renunciant; rather, if one can extensively give rise to the four immeasurable minds and establish sentient beings [in them], this is called renunciation.

It is not by practicing wholesome dharmas for oneself that one is called a renunciant; rather, it is by being able to increase the roots of goodness in sentient beings that one is called a renunciant.
It is not by attaining entry into nirvana for oneself that one is called a renunciant; rather, it is by desiring to establish all sentient beings in great parinirvāṇa that one is a renunciant.
One does not become a renunciant merely by eliminating afflictions for oneself; rather, one is called a renunciant by diligently severing the afflictions of all sentient beings.
One does not become a renunciant merely by being able to protect one’s own body and mind; rather, one is called a renunciant by protecting all sentient beings.
One does not become a renunciant merely by liberating oneself from the bonds of body and mind; one is called a renunciant because one liberates all sentient beings from the bonds of body and mind.

One does not become a renunciant merely by attaining liberation for oneself from the terrors of birth and death; one is called a renunciant because one can remove the terrors of birth and death for all sentient beings and cause them to attain liberation.

One does not become a renunciant merely by seeking one's own nirvana for personal happiness; rather, one is called a renunciant because of diligently practicing vigor in order to cause all sentient beings to fulfill all Buddha-dharmas.

Mañjuśrī said: "O maiden! As for one who has left the household life, to give rise to a mind of loving-kindness and compassion toward all sentient beings is what is called 'leaving the household life.'"
One who has left the household life does not perceive the evils of any sentient beings nor grasp at their characteristics; this is called "leaving the household life.
One who has left the household life does not expose the faults of others, but instructs those who possess a sense of shame and remorse to repent; this is called "leaving the household life."
"Daughter! For those who have left the household life, it is difficult; they are said to be 'belonging to others.
A bodhisattva is not so, for their body and mind are autonomous and free from any attachment."
The woman asked:
"In what sense is it said that one who has gone forth is 'belonging to another'? Mañjuśrī replied:
"One who belongs to the precepts is called a renunciant; one who violates the precepts is not called a renunciant.
One who belongs to samādhi is called a renunciant; one with a distracted mind is not called a renunciant.
One who belongs to wisdom is called a renunciant; one who is deluded is not called a renunciant."
"One who belongs to liberation is called a renunciant; one who is apart from liberation is not called a renunciant. The woman said, "Mañjuśrī!
“What is meant by a bodhisattva being ‘not dependent on others’?
Mañjuśrī replied, “A bodhisattva’s internal self-realization of the Dharma is not learned from another; this is called ‘not dependent on others. Why is that? Because...”
"Because the Bodhisattva attains self-awakening and understanding regarding all-knowledge.

At that time, after Mañjuśrī had spoken these words on the dharma of renunciation, five hundred bodhisattvas felt great joy in their hearts; they immediately removed the garments and necklaces from their bodies and offered them to Mañjuśrī, praising him, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
"Please explain this Dharma, and I shall practice it.

At that time, Mañjuśrī said to the girl Suvarṇavarṇā, "You should mount the chariot and convert the son of the householder Mahātejas; if you can convert this son of the householder, that itself shall be called 'leaving home'."
When Mañjuśrī had spoken these words, the entire assembly was filled with doubt and wonder, each thinking to themselves:
"This woman has already abandoned desire; for what reason, then, does he send her to be together with one who possesses desire?"
At that time, the Golden-Colored Girl, perceiving that doubt had arisen in the minds of the great assembly, addressed them, saying:
“Although the Bodhisattva Free from Greed constantly dwells together with those who are greedy, he remains free from ill repute because he teaches and transforms them;
although the Bodhisattva himself is free from hatred and delusion, even when dwelling together with those possessed of them, he likewise incurs no ill repute because he teaches and transforms them.”
The Bodhisattva, having personally transcended afflictions, dwells among those who possess them; yet for the sake of teaching and transforming them, he remains free from ill repute.

Just as a mother and her child dwell together constantly without mutual defilement, so too is the Bodhisattva free from greed: though dwelling among those who are greedy, he is always undefiled by greed.

For example, just as a eunuch has no lustful attachment even when in the company of women, so too the bodhisattva, having distanced himself from the three realms, remains free from desire even while acting within the realm of desire.

At that time, the Golden Girl clearly understood the afflictions and evil dharmas of birth and death; she dwelt at the limit of detachment from desire, attained the light of detachment, and removed the darkness of desire. Having prostrated at the feet of Mañjuśrī and circumambulated him three times to the right, she was about to mount her chariot when she spoke these verses:
"Now as I mount my chariot, I am free from the three poisons; My essential nature is pure and without greedy attachment.
Far removed from anger, I possess a heart of compassion; Free from further delusion, I have attained wisdom."
My thoughts of craving have now been purified; I shall now mount my chariot and go to the forest.
Formerly, I was intoxicated by a mind of craving, clinging to wealth and beauty without awareness, like a great cloud covering the earth, so that the sun’s light did not emerge or shine.
That light neither goes nor comes; it is hidden and does not appear because it is covered by great clouds.
Likewise, when sentient beings are shrouded by afflictions (*kleśa*), the pure great wisdom does not shine.
That wisdom neither comes nor goes; once the afflictions are known, the light of wisdom emerges.
Nor does it come from any other place.
Through pure contemplation, afflictions are extinguished; name-and-form is neither grasped nor abandoned, neither arising nor ceasing, and neither given to others nor taken by them.
Such is the flavor of the Dharma, utterly pure.
That darkness neither departs nor arrives; likewise, wisdom is free from afflictions, yet those afflictions neither depart nor arrive, being neither produced nor extinguished.
Just as a skilled physician treats all manner of ailments, removing only adventitious illnesses so that they do not arise again,
yet without treating the fundamental elements of earth, water, and wind;
so too does one treat the diseases of affliction in all sentient beings, so that through the conditions of wisdom, afflictions no longer exist.
Defilements do not depart, nor is the Dharma lost;
likewise, the various elements and sense-bases remain complete. Previously, I was intermingled with defilements, but now I have distanced myself from them all and attained purity.
At that time, after Mañjuśrī had taught the Dharma and transformed the great assembly within the multitude, the assembly rejoiced.
Mañjuśrī praised them, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
"Listen to the Dharma with a sincere heart.
Having offered this praise, he spoke thus to the great assembly:
"I shall go today to the presence of the Tathāgata. If you, members of the great assembly, wish to hear the Dharma, you should likewise proceed to the Buddha's abode."
Having spoken these words, Mañjuśrī and the great assembly each returned to their respective abodes.
At that time, the maiden Suvarṇavarṇā, surrounded before and behind by eighty female attendants, mounted a precious chariot together with the son of the elder and proceeded toward the grove.

Having arrived at the grove, they set up variously adorned jeweled banners, streamers, and canopies, as well as fragrant flowers, necklaces, and hundred-jeweled incense burners throughout the trees. For the sake of pleasure, they performed music, song, dance, and laughter, and further provided various kinds of sweet and delicious food and drink.

At that time, the maiden Suvarṇavarṇā lay sleeping with her head resting upon the knees of the elder’s son, Ugratejas. By means of his supernormal power, he manifested the signs of death at the place where she lay; she became bloated, putrid, and rotten, such that it was difficult even to approach her. In an instant, her abdomen burst open and her liver and intestines were torn asunder; the five viscera were exposed, foul and loathsome. Impurities flowed from the passages of her excrement and urine. From her eyes, ears, nose, and all parts of her body, including every pore, pus and blood gushed out in profusion. Her mouth emitted a foul stench, and the pervasive odor of her bloated and putrid body permeated the entire grove. Her skull fractured and the brain spilled out, spreading over her limbs and joints. Blue flies fed upon her, and maggots wriggled about; the various kinds of filth and corruption were beyond description.
At that time, the son of the householder saw this corpse; great terror arose within him and the hair on his body stood on end.
He thought to himself: "Now I am here without rescue and without refuge; looking in all four directions, there is no place of reliance. My fear redoubles, and I let out a cry of great terror."
That son of a householder experienced great terror for two reasons:

first, because he had never before witnessed such a terrifying event, he was struck with fear; second, because the great assembly knew that he had come here together with the other and now suddenly died, they would suspect him of having killed him intentionally. Fearing that King Ajātaśatru might fail to discern this truth and instead impose a wrongful execution upon him, he was filled with dread.
At that time, the son of the elder was alone in this forest and did not see a single person. He further thought to himself:
"I am now filled with fear; among the śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, and others, who is able to save me?"

Although that son of a householder’s past roots of goodness had matured, because he had not heard or seen the Dharma taught by Mañjuśrī together with the Golden Woman, Mañjuśrī immediately employed his supernormal powers to cause all the trees in the grove to speak these verses:
“The essential nature of all phenomena is as the householder has perceived it:
the three realms are entirely illusory; like a phantom, they are all unreal.”
Covered by skin, it is foul and impure; yet the ordinary person has no sense of shame.
Due to the causes and conditions of evil perceptions, delusory thoughts give rise to craving and attachment.
It is like a jar filled with excrement, yet outwardly adorned with painted ornaments.
Out of ignorance and folly, one takes up a jar and wears it upon the head.
When it falls to the ground, it immediately breaks; impurities fill it completely, and its various foul odors are unbearable.
Only then does the mind feel regret and seek to cast it away.
In this way, all ordinary people falsely discriminate regarding female form;
seeing it as long or short, red or white, they become stained by passion due to evil perceptions.
If one sees the true nature of the body, you will find that your own body is likewise so.
Who that possesses true insight would conceive attachment for a stinking corpse?
You should not fear now; this nature of phenomena is empty, and all things are not real.
Why is it that you, who were previously so attached, now feel such fear?
[I am] able to bestow peace and happiness upon you; among all those who preach the Dharma, I am supreme, for I declare that all sensual desires are impermanent.
Like clouds, mist, and lightning, the five desires are deceptive and unreal; what wise person would be attached to them?
Just as wind stirs the water to produce foam and bubbles, there is no substantial agent therein;
they arise only through the conjunction of causes and conditions.
Thus, these phenomena of name-and-form (nāmarūpa) Have no real agent;
yet, through the power of karma, they are not lost, But arise from the conjunction of various dharmas.
That exquisite form seen in the past— Where has it gone now?
Whence does this foul form come, that such great terror arises?
This dharma does not abide in any direction, nor does it come from elsewhere;
it does not go away to the future, yet it is visible because it arises through aggregation.
Within that, there is no agent, nor is there any real experiencer;
apart from the phenomena of acting and experiencing, it is like an illusion—empty and without reality.
You should not give rise to fear toward the bodies of others.
If you can observe for yourself that your own body is likewise so—
just like the sensual pleasures in a dream that cause one to leap for joy and great delight—
the person who clings to sensual pleasures is no different from those in a dream.
Your fear cannot be dispelled, nor is there anyone to offer you comfort;
you should now go quickly to the Great Teacher, the Tathāgata.
This great terror of yours cannot be overcome by parents or kinsmen.
Knowledge is that which can save;
it can uproot the very foundation [of suffering], bestow fearlessness upon those in fear,
and protect those who have no protector.
"You should take refuge in the Buddha, and likewise in the sublime Dharma and Saṅgha.
Those who take refuge in them will be liberated from all fears and swiftly attain the state of gods and humans."

At that time, having heard these verses, the elder’s son Mahātejas was filled with immense joy and leaped for joy beyond measure; deeply congratulating himself, he abandoned the corpse and emerged from the forest.

At that time, the Buddha was atop Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa; knowing that the son of a householder’s roots of goodness were mature and he was capable of being transformed through instruction, he emitted a great radiance, the light of which shone everywhere throughout the kingdom of Magadha.
At that time, within the radiance, the son of the elder saw from afar the body of the Buddha, like the rising sun, surrounded by a great assembly as he preached the Dharma.

Having seen this, he called the Buddha to mind with single-minded devotion; suddenly, he again beheld a staircase made of the seven treasures with railings on all sides leading to the Buddha’s location, and he also saw exquisite flowers strewn everywhere along the path.
At that time, the son of the elder set out on the road intending to go; as he first began to walk, Śakra Devānām Indra immediately blocked his path, standing in the way and saying:
"O son of the elder, you wish to go and see the Buddha to obtain great and wholesome benefit, and the Buddha also takes pity upon you; I shall accompany you to the place where the Buddha is."
Then the son of the householder immediately went with Śakra to the place where the Buddha was.
Having arrived at the Buddha’s presence, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, took the *mandārava* flowers from his robe-sack and instructed the son of the householder to scatter them over the Buddha.

Then, having received the celestial flowers, the son of the elder gave rise to a heart of joy and scattered them over the Buddha. He prostrated with his head at the Buddha's feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and standing to one side, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I now take refuge in the Buddha with a sincere heart!"
"I take refuge in the Dharma!
I take refuge in the Saṅgha!
Having performed the threefold refuge, he speaks these words:
"By means of these roots of goodness and various merits, may I attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi in a future life.
Then he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
This woman of golden hue is well known to the assembly; desiring pleasure, I gave her wealth and jewels so that we might go together to the grove to enjoy ourselves.

Upon reaching that forest, she lay down resting upon my lap and suddenly died. Immediately thereafter, she became putrid, decayed, and foul-smelling, becoming terrifying to behold; all the attendants who had accompanied her abandoned me and departed, and none remained to see her.
"I fear that King Ajātaśatru, learning of this woman's death, will suspect me of the murder and subject me to arbitrary execution; for this reason, I now feel great terror.
At that time, the Buddha said to the son of the householder:
"Do not be anxious or afraid; I shall grant you all-fearlessness."
"Son of a householder, one who takes refuge in the Buddha has nothing to fear in any place.
He further said: "You should relinquish the causes and conditions of fear."
Then the son of the householder addressed the Buddha,
saying, “From what do all fears arise?
The Buddha said:
“Fear arises due to the causes and conditions of greed, hatred, and delusion;
fear arises due to the cause and condition of the view of a self-identity;
fear arises due to the cause and condition of wrong views.”
Fear arises due to the condition of craving;
fear arises due to the condition of "I" and "mine";
fear arises due to the condition of attachment.
Fear arises due to the causes and conditions of strife and contention;
fear arises due to the causes and conditions of attachment to one's own self;
and fear arises because of conceiving the notion of permanence within the impermanent.
Fear arises because one conceives the notion of pleasure within phenomena that are suffering;
fear arises because one conceives the notion of purity within what is impure;
and fear arises because one conceives the notion of a self within what is non-self.
Fear arises because of attachment to the causes and conditions of the five aggregates;
fear arises because one does not contemplate the twelve bases;
fear arises because one does not contemplate the eighteen elements.
Fear arises because one does not see future evils;
fear arises because one does not contemplate the internal and external causes and conditions of the body;
fear arises because of attachment to the causes and conditions of life.
"O son of a householder!
For such causes and conditions as these, all fears arise; you should relinquish such matters.
He spoke further, saying:
"Do you see these various evils within this woman's body?
The son of the householder replied,
"Indeed, World-Honored One!"
"I have now seen it.
The Buddha said, "It is so;
all dharmas are impermanent and subject to decay, suffering, empty, and unreal—they are merely deceptive."

Because they do not know that all things arise through the conditions of karma, they are like illusions—unreal and devoid of form and characteristics; like dreams—wherein joy and pleasure have no true reality; like mirages in the heat—where there is no water, yet one perceives it as such; like reflections on water—shining upon a wall, moving when the water moves, yet having no coming or going; like images in a mirror—produced by the power of karma; like the moon in water—appearing when the water is still, yet having no coming or going; like echoes—arising from sound and incapable of being described as real; like shadows—inincapable of being grasped; like illusions—their essential nature is empty;
and like the wind—its nature cannot be seized. Thus, all phenomena are provisional and unreal, neither increasing nor decreasing.
Thus it is, son of a householder!
You should know that all phenomena have no master and no agent; there is no one who grasps them.
Where now is that thought of desire you previously had?
The son of the elder said:

"What is seen here—lengths, shortnesses, beautiful colors, and so forth—is that to which ordinary people become greedily attached due to the causes and conditions of false perceptions; such things do not exist within the Noble Dharma."
"In the Dharma of the Sage, it is simply that which is impure; because one sees it as it truly is, because one is free from evil thoughts, and because greed, hatred, and delusion are exhausted.
The Buddha said:
"Excellent, excellent!"
"Son of a householder!

By seeing the nature of greed, one leaves behind evil thoughts and reflections; by leaving behind evil thoughts, greed, hatred, and delusion are exhausted. Therefore, you should give rise to a pure mind and cultivate skillful practices, engendering the activity of wisdom regarding all objects, and remain free from the view of self and the view of others."
The son of the elder said,
"How does a bodhisattva give rise to a pure mind and practice the conduct of wisdom?
The Buddha said:
“Son of a householder!

A bodhisattva should seek awakening within the very nature of greed; likewise, they should seek awakening within the nature of hatred and delusion, and also seek awakening within the nature of all afflictions. Since the nature of greed, hatred, delusion, and all such afflictions is empty and insubstantial, the bodhisattva’s practice of wisdom arises within all phenomena.”
Therefore, son of a householder!

That nature of greed, hatred, and delusion has no root, nor does it have a place of abiding; it has no master and no agent. It is pure within and without, empty and non-existent, devoid of self, devoid of sentient beings, and devoid of life-span. It is signless because it is free from the *pudgala*; it is wishless because it is free from evil discursive thoughts; and it is free from grasping because it is free from craving and attachment.
Because the intrinsic nature of greed, hatred, and delusion is non-arising, the bodhisattva gives rise to the practice of wisdom regarding all phenomena.
"Furthermore, son of a householder!
For the Bodhisattva who practices the skillful means of pure focal objects, there is bodhi within all mental phenomena that arise. Why is this?

If that mind is formless and free from form, free from conceptual discrimination, its essential nature is like an illusion, and it does not continue as a succession between self and other, internal and external, this is called bodhi.
Furthermore, son of a householder!
A bodhisattva should not awaken to other matters, but only awaken to his own mind. Why is this?
To awaken to one's own mind is to awaken to the minds of all sentient beings.
If one's own mind is pure, then the minds of all sentient beings are likewise pure.
As is the essential nature of one's own mind, so is the essential nature of the minds of all sentient beings;
as is the freedom from defilement of one's own mind, so is the freedom from defilement of the minds of all sentient beings;
as is the freedom from greed of one's own mind, so is the freedom from greed of the minds of all sentient beings.
Just as one's own mind is free from hatred, so too is the mind of all sentient beings free from hatred;
just as one's own mind is free from delusion, so too is the mind of all sentient beings free from delusion;
just as one's own mind is free from afflictions, so too is the mind of all sentient beings free from afflictions.
To give rise to this awakening is called the awakening of the knowledge of all modes of knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*).

Thus, a bodhisattva who practices the skillful means of pure focalization is able to know that the essential nature of afflictions (*kleśa*) defiles the minds of all sentient beings. If there are those who say that adventitious afflictions (*āgantuka-kleśa*) continuously defile the mind, the bodhisattva, through his skillful means regarding phenomena, is well able to teach and transform those sentient beings without causing them any distress or confusion.
"If those sentient beings awaken to adventitious afflictions, even adventitious afflictions cannot defile them.
After the Buddha had spoken this Dharma, the son of the elder attained the patience that accords with the Dharma (anulomikī kṣānti).

At that time, the maiden Suvarṇavarṇā, knowing that the son of the elder had been converted and instructed, adorned five hundred horse-drawn chariots and surrounded them on all sides; with various kinds of music being played and sung, she proceeded to the place where the Buddha was.
Having arrived, he descended from his carriage, prostrated himself three times with his head to the ground, circumambulated her three times to the right,
and then stood to one side. At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī asked the son of the elder,
"Do you recognize this sister?"
The son of the householder said,
"I truly recognize it now. Mañjuśrī said:
“How do you perceive them?
At that time, the son of the elder addressed Mañjuśrī with these verses:
“I see forms as like foam on water, And all sensations as like bubbles.”
I perceive her as being like a mirage; thus do I know her.
I see her conduct as being like a plantain tree; I know consciousness to be like an illusion.
The name "woman" is a mere conventional designation; thus do I know her.
The body is without sensation, like wood, And likewise like grass, tiles, or rubble;
The mind cannot be seen— Thus do I recognize it.
It is not a self, nor a sentient being, Nor a life-force, nor a person (pudgala).
The continuity of the eighteen elements—thus do I know them.
Within them there is neither greed nor hatred, nor is there delusion;
they are neither defiled nor pure—thus do I know them.
All ordinary beings are like those intoxicated, giving rise to perverted and evil thoughts;
they do not defile the wise, and thus I recognize them.
Like corpses in a forest, stinking, rotting, foul, and impure.
Such is the nature of the body; such do I know it to be.
The past was originally not extinguished, the future will not arise, and the present does not abide even for a moment; such do I know it to be.
Mañjuśrī, listen well: that kindness is difficult to repay.
Originally I was full of greed and desire, yet upon seeing [him], I attained liberation through the contemplation of impurity.
His body did not truly die; he manifested death only to transform me.
Out of compassion for the multitudes, he manifests these forms; who, upon seeing them, would not give rise to the resolve for enlightenment?
Such are greed, hatred, and delusion, as well as all afflictions—this nature of phenomena is truly excellent and most subtle.
At that time, the Tathāgata smiled, and from his face issued forth light of five colors, which illuminated the trichiliocosm; having done so, it returned and entered through the crown of his head.

At that time, having seen this light, Ānanda rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and praised him, saying:
“Excellent, World-Honored One!”
For what reason and by what causal conditions do you manifest a smile?
The Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas do not manifest a smile without cause or condition.
The Buddha said to Ānanda,
“Do you see this golden-colored girl? Ānanda replied:
“Yes, I have seen her.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

“This girl Suvarṇavarṇā was already taught and inspired by Mañjuśrī in the past to resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; now, once again, through hearing the True Dharma from Mañjuśrī, she has attained the *anulomikī-kṣānti* (receptive patience in accordance with the Dharma).”
The Buddha said to Ānanda,
"Do you see this son of a householder, Ugravarman? Ānanda replied:
“Yes, I have seen it. The Buddha said, “Ānanda!

"This son of a householder was already taught and inspired by me in the past to resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; now, having heard the true Dharma from me, he has attained the patient acceptance of the Dharma (*dharmanidhyāna-kṣānti*)."

Ānanda! This woman, Suvarṇavarṇā, after ninety hundred thousand kalpas in a future age, shall attain Buddhahood under the name Ratnaprabha Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, with an immeasurable lifespan.
That buddha-world shall be named Ratnaguṇa-kṣetra, and the eon shall be named Sukhajanman.

When that daughter attains buddhahood in the future, the clothing, food and drink, lifespan, and physical appearance of the sentient beings in that land will all be equal to those of the various heavenly kings of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, without any difference whatsoever.
In that buddha-world, there are no śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas; it consists purely of the jewels of the bodhisattvas of the Mahāyāna.

When that Tathāgata Ratnaprabha attains buddhahood, this son of a householder will obtain the body of a bodhisattva named Guṇaprabha. He will uphold the treasury of the Buddha’s Dharma, receiving and maintaining all the treasuries of the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata Ratnaprabha.
When the Tathāgata Ratnaprabha was approaching parinirvāṇa, he bestowed the prediction of enlightenment upon the Bodhisattva Guṇaprabha and addressed the great assembly:

"After my parinirvāṇa and after my Dharma has ceased, this Bodhisattva Guṇaprabha shall attain Buddhahood, known by the name Ratnajvāla Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān."

When the Tathāgata had thus bestowed the prediction upon the two individuals, at that moment the trichiliocosm shook in six ways, and a great radiance was emitted, pervading all worlds throughout the ten directions.
When this Dharma of bestowing predictions was being taught, eight thousand people and others resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, the Elder Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"What should this sutra be named?
The Buddha said, "This sutra is named 'The Dharma Gate of Great Adornment'; it should be upheld in this way."
It is also titled "The Scripture on the Power of Mañjuśrī’s Miraculous Agility," and it is also titled "The Scripture on the Conversion of the Girl Suvarṇavarṇaprabhāsāśrī."

When this sutra had been spoken, the Venerable Ānanda, the girl Suvarṇavarṇā, the son of a householder, Mañjuśrī, and the entire great assembly—including devas, humans, asuras, and others—rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
The Scripture on the Dharma Gate of Great Adornment, Scroll II.
